title: Technical deep dive: Multi-region routing & failover
summary: Deep technical session on multi-region routing, failover policies, capacity planning, and DR playbooks for inference. Covered policy routing, health checks, DNS vs Anycast vs proxy-based failover, KV cache warming, batching tradeoffs across regions, quantization fallbacks, and security constraints for VPC/on-prem. Action items: share playbook, benchmark plan, runbook template, and sample configs.

transcript:
Meeting header:
[00:00] Alex Kim: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. This is Alex from Redwood, AE on the account, with Priya our SE. We planned a deep dive on multi-region routing and failover for your inference footprint.
[00:12] Michael Chen: Hey Alex, thanks. From Atlas side Michael here, CTO, and I have Sara from platform and Daniel our SRE. Priya Nair from security will jump in later.
[00:20] Priya Desai: Quick note: this call will be somewhat deep - we'll talk about policy routing, capacity, KV cache behavior and warmers, batching, quantization fallbacks, and operational runbooks.
[00:32] Sara Lopez: Great. We care mostly about latency for patient-facing APIs in US-EAST and EU-WEST, but we need DR for APAC. Cost is important but safety and compliance first.
[00:42] Daniel Ruiz: Also, our VPC constraints: private peering only, limited egress, and we need KMS integration for keys on any cross-region traffic.
[00:50] Alex Kim: Okay noted. Let's start with routing policies. High-level options: active-active with latency-based routing, primary-secondary with failover, and policy routing by cost/tier.
[01:05] Priya Desai: Active-active means traffic is geo-steered based on latency and we rely on per-region capacity and KV cache locality. That gives lowest latency but you need warm caches everywhere or accept first-request penalty.
[01:22] Michael Chen: Right, warm cache everywhere sounds expensive. Can you quantify cache warm-up costs?
[01:28] Priya Desai: Rough ballpark: if you fully warm prefix KV caches for a 2M req/day workload, eager warming could double tokens served during warm-up. More realistic pattern: warm most common prefixes and accept misses for long-tail. We can do traffic-aware cache warmers that prepopulate popular prefixes across regions.
[01:46] Sara Lopez: How does batching interact with that? We batch at the proxy layer, yes?
[01:52] Priya Desai: There are two layers: client side or gateway batching and runtime continuous batching inside the GPU worker. For multi-region, batching adds complexity because latency budgets differ. If you route to closest region, batching windows are tighter. In failover scenario, a surge to a secondary region can increase batching window which could help throughput but hurt tail latency.
[02:14] Daniel Ruiz: So for our SLAs (100ms p95 text gen endpoint) we might prefer smaller batches and more dedicated capacity?
[02:20] Priya Desai: Correct. For p95~100ms you want lower batching latency and more GPU reservations. Redwood Dedicated gives predictable throughput; for hosted we suggest reserved pools or capacity pins for critical endpoints.
[02:33] Alex Kim: Let's talk failover mechanics: DNS-based failover, Anycast, and proxy-based routing with health checks. Pros/cons?
[02:41] Priya Desai: DNS is simple but has TTL and cache issues; slow to converge. Anycast depends on network providers and can be hard with private VPC peering. Proxy approach (global control plane + regional proxies) lets us do fast per-request failover with circuit breakers, but requires a small control plane footprint and peered connectivity.
[03:00] Michael Chen: For Atlas we use VPC peering to Redwood private endpoints in each region; DNS changes take too long and our clients sit behind customer firewalls. Proxy-based sounds better.
[03:12] Priya Desai: Then you can implement short-circuit health checks: e.g., synthetic in-flight checks to GPU worker and KV store, with circuit-breaker open when error rate crosses threshold. We recommend exponential backoff and overflow queues rather than immediate drop.
[03:26] Sara Lopez: How do you prefer to handle session affinity/sticky routing for KV cache locality? We have user session affinity for some endpoints.
[03:34] Priya Desai: Consistent hashing at the proxy layer can keep affinity, but on failover you need to rebuild mapping which invalidates cache locality. Alternative is sticky by user-region with fallback to nearest healthy region, and a cache warmer to mitigate misses.
[03:49] Daniel Ruiz: Any notes about model variants and quantization in failover? We might serve a quantized variant in secondary region to save memory.
[03:57] Priya Desai: Yes, that's common. Policy idea: on failover, route to cheaper quantized variant with graceful degradation of quality. Need to ensure tokenizer, output schema consistent. Also, KV cache layout may differ across quantization variants; make sure KV cache keys are compatible or have translation layer.
[04:16] Alex Kim: Also important: automated model fallback list per region, e.g., full FP16 model in primaries, int8 quantized fallback in backups. We store model compatibility matrix in control plane.
[04:27] Michael Chen: If secondary is quantized, how do we measure/regress quality? We need canary metrics.
[04:33] Priya Desai: Redwood Optimize integrates quality monitors and can compare outputs vs baseline on small eval sets; during failover you can toggle shadowing to measure model drift and alert if quality drops below threshold.
[04:45] Sara Lopez: Network constraints: our peering limits cross-region egress; is it possible to route only failover traffic across regions?
[04:53] Priya Desai: Absolutely - route by policy: geo-primary strict routing for normal ops, and only when health-check or capacity thresholds breached route e.g., 5-10% spillover to other region, or full cutover for DR. That minimizes egress.
[05:06] Daniel Ruiz: Capacity planning question: how does autoscaling behave across regions under a global surge?
[05:13] Priya Desai: Each region autoscale independently; you can use global orchestration to trigger scale ops in multiple regions. For spikes, we recommend buffer capacity (reserved instances) and autoscale with faster scale-up for critical endpoints. Also, implement rate-limiting and shedding policies as last resort.
[05:29] Alex Kim: Let's go through an example DR playbook scenario - primary us-east fails (AZ/region outage) and traffic shifts to eu-west and us-west. What steps?
[05:40] Priya Desai: Step 1: detection via synthetic and real traffic health probes. Step 2: mark us-east as degraded in control plane, enable traffic steering rules to shift N% to other regions. Step 3: warm KV cache for most used prefixes in receiving regions using historical traffic. Step 4: ensure quantized fallback variant is available if primary model not available. Step 5: enable circuit breakers and adjust batching windows to maintain p95. Step 6: telemetry and canary checks to validate responses. And finally, revert once primary healthy and drain traffic gradually.
[06:10] Michael Chen: How long before warmers make a meaningful difference?
[06:14] Priya Desai: Depends on working set. For top 10% prefixes, warmers can pre-populate in minutes if you parallelize. For long-tail, may take hours. We usually accept a hybrid: warm top prefixes immediately and let background warming continue.
[06:27] Sara Lopez: What's the RTO/RPO realistic target for this type of setup?
[06:31] Priya Desai: RTO maybe in the order of minutes to low tens of minutes depending on DNS, peering, and warming. RPO for inference stateless APIs is typically zero; for stateful KV caches you accept cache miss fallback - so RPO is acceptable as long as upstream data is durable.
[06:47] Daniel Ruiz: Are there automated failover test frameworks? We want to run game days.
[06:51] Priya Desai: Yes, we recommend game days: simulated region outage, synthetic traffic reroutes, and canary validation. Redwood provides a failover simulator that can flip routing policies and run synthetic workloads to validate latency/throughput. We'll share the script.
[07:03] Alex Kim: Security/Compliance: Priya Nair from customer will want KMS integration, audit trails, and SSO scoping. Any blockers for private deployments?
[07:12] Priya Desai: For Redwood Private we can deploy the control plane inside a customer VPC with KMS/HSM integration and forward logs to your SIEM. For peered hosted endpoints we support envelope encryption and audit logs. We need to validate network ACLs and port allowlists.
[07:26] Priya Nair (joining): Sorry for being late. Quick Q: is cross-region traffic encrypted by default and do we support key rotation without downtime?
[07:33] Alex Kim: Yes encrypted in transit; we support KMS key rotation with rolling re-encryption and no service downtime for inference (we do key swapping at worker restart windows). We'll share the KMS integration doc.
[07:44] Priya Nair: Good. Also need SOC2 evidence for runbook testing and game days.
[07:49] Alex Kim: We can provide audit logs and test reports; Priya from our side will coordinate the evidence package.
[07:56] Sara Lopez: Back to technical: health checks - what are the recommended probes?
[07:59] Priya Desai: Multi-level: (1) Liveness on worker process, (2) lightweight inference ping (small token request), (3) KV store latency check, (4) GPU memory healthy, (5) queue depth. Combine into a single health status with severity mapping.
[08:16] Daniel Ruiz: How fast should we treat a worker as unhealthy? We don't want false positives on brief GC pauses.
[08:21] Priya Desai: Use rolling windows and require sustained failure for, say, 15s for critical checks and 60s for non-critical. That avoids flapping. Also use circuit-breaker thresholds by error type.
[08:32] Alex Kim: Observatory: Redwood Console will surface per-model latency, cost per token, and per-route breakdown so you can see spillover and regen costs.
[08:40] Michael Chen: Great. Can we get an example config for envoy/proxy rules for failover and consistent hashing?
[08:46] Alex Kim: Yes we'll share that. We'll include sample envoy config with hash policies and cluster failover weight adjustments.
[08:53] Sara Lopez: A few quick specifics about quantization and KV compatibility: what happens if int8 model uses different KV key derivation?
[08:59] Priya Desai: Key derivation must be identical across variants; otherwise you either maintain variant-specific caches (costly) or provide a translation layer that maps keys. We prefer consistent derivation and compatibility testing during model onboarding.
[09:12] Daniel Ruiz: Are there specific metrics you recommend tracking during failover?
[09:16] Priya Desai: Track p50/p95/p99, queue depth, GPU utilization, cache hit rate, model error rate (if you have evals), request success rate, and tail latency increase. Also track cross-region egress and cost delta.
[09:29] Michael Chen: For our compliance audits we need a written DR runbook we can include in binder. Can Redwood provide a template?
[09:34] Alex Kim: Yes we'll provide a DR runbook template and a sample incident timeline.
[09:38] Priya Desai: I'll also attach a checklist for canarying quantized variants and a simple test harness.
[09:44] Sara Lopez: About warmers - do warmers need service account credentials and will they be run from control plane?
[09:49] Priya Desai: Warmers can be run from control plane or customer-run jobs. For private deployments we recommend customer-run warmers that pull from historical logs and run in-region with local creds, so you avoid cross-region egress costs.
[10:01] Daniel Ruiz: One tricky point: what about consistency for incremental KV updates if a write goes to the failed region?
[10:08] Priya Desai: Design principle: inference cache should be read-mostly and derived from canonical upstream. Writes should be directed at canonical store (global DB), and inference caches are eventually consistent. For strong consistency needs, route writes to primary and consider synchronous replication if needed, but that has latency costs.
[10:23] Alex Kim: Let's document a sample policy for routing: default geo-primary (100% to local), spillover policy (on CPU/GPU>80% or latency>p95 threshold): spill 10% then 30% then full; fallback to quantized variant if model not available; for security triggers (cert/key issues) fail closed to private region.
[10:44] Michael Chen: That spillover staircase makes sense. For game days, we want a script to simulate the staircase.
[10:50] Priya Desai: We'll share a simulation script. It increments load and flips routing weights; you can run it against a staging control plane.
[10:58] Sara Lopez: Any mention of cost visibility during failover? We need to show execs the delta.
[11:03] Alex Kim: Redwood Console will surface cost-per-route, and we can produce a cost impact report for simulated failovers. We'll include an estimated cost delta in the benchmark results.
[11:13] Daniel Ruiz: A quick question on telemetry: what trace headers or tags do you recommend for correlating region, model-variant, and cache-hit?
[11:20] Priya Desai: Include tags: region, cluster_id, model_variant, cache_hit:boolean, batch_size, request_id. That gives good correlation for root cause.
[11:29] Michael Chen: Ok, last set of logistics: what do you need from us to run the benchmark and pilot?
[11:34] Alex Kim: We'll need: (1) traffic profile and sample payloads, (2) auth/peering details for staging endpoints, (3) expected RTO/RPO and any blackout windows, (4) list of critical endpoints to protect.
[11:47] Sara Lopez: We'll share traffic profiles and staging creds by Friday.
[11:50] Alex Kim: Great. We'll follow up with the playbook + configs + benchmark plan.
[11:55] Michael Chen: Thanks everyone. Any other Qs?
[11:58] Daniel Ruiz: One nit: can we get a note about how you maintain model rollout order across regions? We need consistent ordering for version pinning.
[12:04] Priya Desai: Short answer: control plane supports model pinning per-route and global rollout strategies (canary percentages across regions). We keep a global version map and allow region-specific overrides. We'll include docs.
[12:16] Alex Kim: OK we'll recap next steps. Thanks all.
